source_text: XXIII. Ad hoc Respondent plurimi Christianarum Scholarum Theologi, & recte quidem meo judicio, praescientiam Dei nullam imponere rebus necessitatem: nec enim illam esse rerum causam, sed potius res ipsas futuras illius causam certa ratione dici posse: Videlicet, quia res non ideo futurae sunt, quoniam Deus illas futuras esse praescit; Sed contra Deus illas futuras esse praescit, quia revera futurae sunt.
english: Very many theologians of the Christian schools answer this, and in my judgement rightly, that God's foreknowledge places no necessity on things. Foreknowledge is not the cause of things; rather, in a certain sense the future things themselves can be called its cause.
Things are not future because God foreknows that they will be. On the contrary, God foreknows that they will be because they really are future.

source_text: XXIV. Ad id vero quod objicitur, fieri non posse quin eveniant ea quae Deus ab aeterno praescit esse futura, ac proinde omnia necessario evenire, quandoquidem omnia futura Deus praevidet, ex communi Scholarum sententia dicendum est, impossibile quidem esse ut non eveniant ea quae Deus futura praenovit, sed in sensu composito solum, non autem in sensu diviso. Quibus verbis innuitur non posse simul consistere, ut aliquid sit praevisum a Deo tanquam futurum, & tamen non eveniat; Sed nihilominus, simpliciter, & absolute loquendo, rem illam quae praevisa est posse non evenire, si consideretur ex sua natura, & citra respectum ad Dei praevisionem. Exempli gratia Judas quem Deus praeviderat Christum esse proditurum, poterat tamen, siquidem voluisset, Christum non prodere. Nec Dei praescientia necessitatem illi imposuit prodendi Christum. Neq; inde sequitur potuisse falli praescientiam Dei; quia si Judas Christum non prodidisset, proditio ejus praevisa non fuisset; sed praevidisset Deus Christum a Juda non fuisse prodendum.
english: The objection runs: what God foreknows from eternity as future cannot fail to happen; God foresees all future things; so everything happens necessarily. The common teaching of the schools replies that it is indeed impossible for what God foreknew as future not to happen, but only in the composite sense, not in the divided sense.

This means that two things cannot hold together: that something is foreseen by God as future, and that it does not happen. Yet, speaking simply and absolutely, the thing foreseen is able not to happen, if it is considered in its own nature and without reference to God's foresight.

Take Judas. God had foreseen that he would betray Christ, yet he could have refrained from betraying him had he wished. God's foreknowledge did not lay on him any necessity of betraying Christ. Nor does it follow that God's foreknowledge could have been mistaken. Had Judas not betrayed Christ, his betrayal would not have been foreseen; God would instead have foreseen that Judas was not going to betray Christ.

source_text: XXV. Itaque necesse est quidem omnia illa fieri, quae Deus futura praevidet, supposita semel ista praevisione: quemadmodum necesse est fieri omnia illa, quae nos ipsi fieri videmus, supposita nostra visione. Sed sicut visio nostra non mutat naturam rerum, nec facit ut in se necessarium sit, quod ex sua natura liberum, sive contingens est: quamvis ex hypothesi quod aliquid fieri videmus, non possit illud non esse: sic praevisio Dei nihil immutat in rebus futuris, nec earum libertatem, aut contingentiam tollit: quamvis illud quod futurum a Deo praevidetur, & sic supponitur futurum, non possit non esse futurum. Nam sicut ex hypothesi quod res actu sit, impossibile est eam non esse actu, eodem plane modo ex hypothesi quod res futura sit, fieri non potest ut non sit futura.
english: Once God's foresight is supposed, then, everything he foresees as future must indeed happen. In the same way, once our own seeing is supposed, everything we see happening must be happening.

Our seeing does not alter the nature of things. It does not make something necessary in itself that is free or contingent by its own nature, even though, given that we see it happening, it cannot fail to be. In just the same way God's foresight alters nothing in future things and does not take away their freedom or contingency. This holds even though what God foresees as future, being supposed future, cannot fail to be future.
If we suppose that a thing actually exists, it cannot fail to exist actually. In exactly the same way, if we suppose that a thing is future, it cannot fail to be future.

source_text: XXVI. Uno verbo, sicut ex visione rerum praesentium inducitur quaedam earum necessitas, sed hypothetica tantum, & quae in Scholis dicitur necessitas consequens, sive consequentiae, quaeque optime consistit cum earum libertate, sive contingentia: sic etiam ex rerum futurarum praevisione, sequitur quidem eas necessario eventuras esse, sed necessitate tantum ex hypothesi, & quae dici solet infallibilitatis, quae non obstat quominus in se & absolute liberae sint, & contingentes. Nam si qua necessitas contingentiam & libertatem tollit, illa demum est quae dicitur antecedens atque absoluta, nec solum consequentiae, sed etiam consequentis.
english: In short, seeing present things brings a certain necessity upon them, but only a hypothetical one. The schools call it consequent necessity, or the necessity of the consequence, and it fits perfectly well with their freedom or contingency.

So too the foresight of future things means that they will necessarily happen, but only by a necessity that rests on a hypothesis, usually called the necessity of infallibility. It does not stop them being free and contingent in themselves and absolutely.
The only necessity that removes contingency and freedom is the one called antecedent and absolute, which is a necessity not merely of the consequence but of the consequent as well.

source_text: XXVII. Alii tamen aliter conciliare nituntur Dei praescientiam cum libertate hominis. Falsam enim esse putant hanc propositionem, Quia res futurae sunt, ideo cognoscuntur a Deo: hanc autem esse veram, Quia Deus praescit aliquid esse futurum, ideo futurum est. Nam juxta ipsos scientia Dei est causa rerum. Neque tamen existimant hoc praejudicare hominum libertati. Quia Deus ab aeterno non solum praescit homines hoc aut illud acturos esse, sed etiam praescit modum quo acturi sunt, nempe libere atque contingenter. Ac proinde, posita Dei praescientia, necessario quidem sequitur verbi causa, quod Petrus loquuturus sit, imo ista Dei scientia causa est, suo modo, quod Petrus sic loquuturus; Sed quod locuturus sit, non quovis modo, verum contingenter & libere. Unde inquiunt, ex praescientia Dei potius infertur actuale exercitium libertatis humanae, quam destruatur. Nam talis praescientia non aufert a voluntate Petri loquentis liberam facultatem qua possit non loqui, si velit: imo potius in ea facultatem ejusmodi ponit. Quae est Doctrina eorum qui dicuntur Thomistae recentiores ut apud Didacum Alvarez videre est in summa Operis de Auxiliis gratiae Divinae lib. 1. cap. 11.
english: Others, however, try to reconcile God's foreknowledge with human freedom in another way. They hold false the proposition 'Things are known by God because they are future', and true the proposition 'Something is future because God foreknows that it will be'. On their view God's knowledge is the cause of things.
Yet they do not think this harms human freedom. From eternity God foreknows not only that people will do this or that, but also the manner in which they will act, namely freely and contingently.

So, given God's foreknowledge, it follows necessarily, to take an example, that Peter will speak. Indeed God's knowledge is, in its own way, the cause of Peter's speaking. But it follows that he will speak in a particular manner: contingently and freely. Hence, they say, God's foreknowledge implies the actual exercise of human freedom rather than destroying it. Such foreknowledge does not remove from Peter's will, as he speaks, the free power by which he could refrain from speaking if he wished; rather it places that very power in his will.
This is the teaching of those called the later Thomists, as can be seen in Didacus Alvarez, in the summary of his work on the aids of divine grace, book 1, chapter 11.

source_text: XXVIII. Simplicius autem adhuc & confusius ad hanc difficultatem respondent ex Doctoribus Reformatis nonnulli, Dei praescientiam rebus omnibus futuris necessitatem quidem aliquam inducere, sed non omnem necessitatem cum libertate pugnare; verum illam duntaxat quae est a coactione, aut a determinatione Physica.
english: Some Reformed teachers answer the difficulty in a still simpler and less precise way. They say that God's foreknowledge does bring a certain necessity upon all future things, but that not every necessity is at odds with freedom. Only necessity arising from compulsion or from physical determination conflicts with it.

source_text: XXIX. Et sic quidem variis modis ostendere conantur Christiani Theologi, quomodo posita futurorum omnium in Deo praescientia, stare possit humana libertas. Sed non minor est difficultas in explicando quomodo posita libertate, qua creaturae possint agere, & non agere, eorum futuri actus possint a Deo praevideri certo & infallibiliter. Quomodo enim certo cognosci potest quod neque in se, neque in causis suis, certam habet existentiam; sed tam non esse & fieri, quam fieri & esse potest?
english: In these various ways Christian theologians try to show how human freedom can stand alongside God's foreknowledge of all future things.

Yet it is no less difficult to explain the reverse. If creatures have freedom to act or not to act, how can God foresee their future acts with certainty and without fail? How can anything be known with certainty that has no certain existence either in itself or in its causes, and is as able not to be or happen as to happen and be?

source_text: XXX. Ut ex difficultate ista se expediant, multum laborant Scholastici Doctores, & variis modis nituntur exponere, qua ratione Deus futura contingentia & libera praesciat. Et primo quidem illi, qui modo jam dicti sunt, Thomistae recentiores, certitudini isti qua Deus ab aeterno futura quaelibet contingentia praescit, duo fundamenta praestruunt. Unum est res omnes futuras in aeternitate Deo praesentes esse, non tantum in esse objectivo, sive in esse cognito: sed etiam in esse reali, & secundum proprias suas existentias. Nam, inquiunt, ita se habet Deus in ordine ad futura contingentia, sicut existens in alta specula, ex qua intuetur totam viam in ordine ad transeuntes per illam; licet enim unus pergat post alium, & posterior non videat priorem; ille tamen qui est in specula, omnes simul intuetur, & habet praesentes sibi: ergo similiter Deus habet sibi praesentes in specula aeternitatis omnes res praeteritas, & futuras: licet istae succedant illis. Quae sunt verba Didaci Alvarez lib. 1. c. 8. Ubi praesentiam istam futurorum in aeternitate, inde praeterea probat, quod aeternitas est duratio indivisibilis tota simul existens: ideoque quicquid ullo tempore coexistit aeternitati, illi toti coexistit, & consequenter illi toti praesens est.
english: The scholastic teachers work hard to get out of this difficulty and try in various ways to explain how God foreknows future contingent and free things.

The first are the later Thomists just mentioned. They lay two foundations for the certainty by which God foreknows every future contingent from eternity. The first is that all future things are present to God in eternity, not merely in objective or known being, but in real being, in their own actual existences.

'God,' they say, 'stands toward future contingents like someone on a high watchtower who surveys the whole road and everyone travelling along it. One traveller follows another and the one behind cannot see the one ahead, yet the watcher on the tower sees them all at once and has them present to himself. So likewise God has present to himself, on the watchtower of eternity, all things past and future, though the one succeeds the other.' These are the words of Didacus Alvarez, book 1, chapter 8.

There he further proves this presence of future things in eternity from the fact that eternity is an indivisible duration that exists whole all at once. Whatever coexists with eternity at any time therefore coexists with all of it, and so is present to all of it.

source_text: XXXI. In principio vero capitis sequentis inde colligit, Quod actualis existentia rerum in aeternitate, considerata ex parte divinae aeternitatis, est propria ratio, propter quam Deus certo cognoscit, omnia futura etiam contingentia. Idque quoniam ea quae sunt praesentia cognoscenti, quamvis secundum se contingentia sint, jam considerantur ut determinata, & ut determinate vera in ordine ad illam mensuram, in qua sunt praesentia, & in ordine ad cognitionem, qua ut praesentia sibi cognoscuntur.
english: At the start of the next chapter he draws this conclusion: the actual existence of things in eternity, viewed from the side of God's eternity, is the proper reason why God knows all future things with certainty, contingent ones included.

The reason is that things present to a knower, though contingent in themselves, are already regarded as determinate. They are determinately true with respect to the measure in which they are present, and with respect to the knowledge by which they are known as present.

source_text: XXXII. Alterum fundamentum, quo niti existimant certitudinem divinae scientiae, respectu eorum quae sunt contingenter futura, est absolutum divinae voluntatis decretum. Nam potest etiam, inquit ibidem Alvarez, ex alio capite desumi certitudo scientiae divinae comparatione futurorum contingentium, nimirum ex decreto absoluto, & efficaci suae voluntatis praedeterminantis in particulari omnia futura, etiam libera, cum omnibus suis circumstantiis, si sunt bona, vel ea permittentis si sunt mala. Atque ut clarius explicet quid sit illud decretum efficax voluntatis divinae permittentis mala, Observat in sequentibus duplex decretum praesupponi ex parte Dei ad praescientiam infallibilem peccatorum. Alterum est decretum absolutum producendi actum peccati, in quantum actus & ens est: Alterum vero est decretum non dandi auxilium efficax ad vitandum peccatum, seu decretum permittendi ejus malitiam, quae soli voluntati creatae, seu defectibili tribuitur. Et in his duobus decretis affirmat certo cognosci omnia peccata futura, quoniam Deo deserente & non adjuvante, peccatorem ne cadat, infallibiliter est peccaturus.
english: The second foundation on which they rest the certainty of God's knowledge of things that will happen contingently is the absolute decree of the divine will. In the same place Alvarez says that the certainty of God's knowledge of future contingents can also be drawn from another source. This is the absolute and efficacious decree of his will, which predetermines in detail every future thing, free ones included, with all their circumstances, if they are good, or permits them if they are evil.

To explain more clearly what this efficacious decree permitting evil is, he notes further on that God's infallible foreknowledge of sins presupposes two decrees on God's part. One is an absolute decree to produce the act of sin insofar as it is an act and a being. The other is a decree not to give efficacious help for avoiding the sin, that is, a decree to permit its wickedness, which is attributed to the created or defectible will alone.
In these two decrees, he says, all future sins are known with certainty. If God abandons the sinner and does not help him so that he will not fall, he will infallibly sin.

source_text: XXXIII. At vero sunt alii in Schola Romana Doctores, qui praesentiam istam futurorum in aeternitate, secundum proprias suas existentias, rejicientes ut vanam atque commentitiam, affirmant omnia futura contingentia, tam quae ex causis secundis liberis, quam quae ex aliis causis naturalibus eveniunt, in solo divino decreto, quo illa fieri decrevit, certo & infallibiliter cognosci. Quae opinio multis veteribus Scholasticis tribui solet, Veluti Scoto, Ricardo, Herveo, & Joanni Majori, aliisque non paucis. Atque hanc quoque sententiam amplectuntur Theologi inter Reformatos plurimi, docentes cum Calvino, Deum non alia ratione praevidere quae futura sunt, quam quia ut fierent decrevit: Praesertim vero Gulielmus Tuissus inter Theologos Anglos celeberrimus, istam Calvini Doctrinam pluribus explicat, tuetur & illustrat, tota fere dissertatione de scientia Media, adversus Penotrum & Suaresium.
english: There are, however, other teachers in the Roman school who reject this presence of future things in eternity in their own existences as empty and invented. They hold that every future contingent, whether it comes from free second causes or from other natural causes, is known with certainty and without fail in God's decree alone, by which he decreed that it should happen. This view is usually attributed to many of the older scholastics, such as Scotus, Richard, Hervaeus, John Major and a good number of others.

Very many Reformed theologians also embrace it, teaching with Calvin that God foresees what will happen for no other reason than that he decreed it should happen. William Twisse, among the most celebrated English theologians, sets out, defends and illustrates this teaching of Calvin at length, through almost the whole of his dissertation on middle knowledge, written against Penot and Suárez.

source_text: XXXIV. Sed utraque haec sententia minime probatur plerisque recentioribus Scholae Romanae Theologis. Nec enim solum rejiciunt supra dictam praesentiam futurorum in aeternitate, secundum esse ipsorum reale; sed neque agnoscunt aliquod efficax Dei decretum, quo praedefiniti sint causarum liberarum actus, antecedenter ad propriam ipsarum determinationem. Itaque ut aliquam praescientiae divinae, respectu futurorum contingentium, rationem reddant, alio confugiunt. Et primo quidem nonnulli sunt, qui existimant ea quae contingenter & libere futura sunt, a Deo cognosci in causa proxima, id est, in voluntate non nude sumpta, sed ut applicata est hic & nunc, cum hoc judicio, hoc objecto, hac inclinatione, ac denique cum omnibus aliis quae illam possunt vel impedire, vel determinare ad volendum.
english: Most of the more recent theologians of the Roman school approve of neither view. They reject the presence of future things in eternity in their real being, described above. Nor do they accept any efficacious decree of God by which the acts of free causes are defined in advance, before those causes determine themselves.

So to give some account of God's foreknowledge of future contingents they take refuge elsewhere. First, some hold that what will happen contingently and freely is known by God in its proximate cause. That cause is the will, taken not on its own but as it is engaged here and now: with this judgement, this object and this inclination, and finally with everything else that can either hinder it or determine it to will.

source_text: XXXV. Ad hanc sententiam accedit Bellarminus. Probabile, inquit, nobis videtur, Deum futuras actiones liberas non videre nisi in humana voluntate. Et paulo post, Deus igitur quia perfecte cognoscit omnes propensiones, & totum ingenium animi nostri, & rursum non ignorat omnia, quae illi possunt occurrere in singulis deliberationibus, & denique perspectum habet, quid magis congruum & aptum sit, ut moveat talem animum, tali propensione & ingenio praeditum, infallibiliter colligit, quam in partem sit animus inclinaturus. Quibus subjungit in ipsa contingente causa praecise considerata, nullam esse determinationem: sed tamen si quis conjungat cum causa contingente, vel libera, omnia quae possunt occurrere & impedire, & videat propensiones & aptitudines tum ipsius causae, tum omnium objectorum & circumstantiarum, quod solus Deus facere potest, existet inde aliqua determinatio, & ratione illius verum erit dicere, hoc erit tali tempore. De gratia & libero Arbitrio lib. 4. cap. 15. Responsione ad sextum argumentum.
english: Bellarmine comes close to this view. 'It seems probable to us,' he says, 'that God sees future free actions only in the human will.' A little later he adds: 'God knows perfectly all the inclinations and the whole temper of our mind. He is not unaware of everything that can present itself to it in each deliberation. Finally, he sees clearly what is most fitting and suitable to move such a mind, endowed with such an inclination and temper. Because of all this he infers without fail which way the mind will lean.'

He goes on to say that in the contingent cause, considered strictly by itself, there is no determination. Suppose, however, that someone takes the contingent or free cause together with everything that can present itself and get in the way. Suppose too that he sees the inclinations and aptitudes both of the cause and of all the objects and circumstances, which God alone can do. Then some determination will result, and because of it one will be able to say truly, 'This will happen at such a time.' On Grace and Free Choice, book 4, chapter 15, in the reply to the sixth argument.

source_text: XXXVI. Alii vero simpliciter dicunt Deum certo praenosse futura contingentia, quia quicquid aliquando est, sive contingenter, sive necessario, antequam esset, verum fuit esse futurum: quicquid autem verum est certo cognoscit intellectus divinus; quoniam nulla veritas latere potest intellectum infinitum, qualis divinus est. Itaque juxta ipsos, Certitudo divinae praescientiae ex duplici capite petenda est. Primo ex infinita vi & perspicacitate divini intellectus. Secundo ex determinata veritate futurorum contingentium. Quae sunt verba Becani Jesuitae, in summa Theologiae tomo 1. tractatu 1. cap. 10. quaest. 11. conclusione prima.
english: Others say simply that God foreknows future contingents with certainty for this reason: whatever exists at some time, whether contingently or necessarily, was true as a future thing before it existed. Whatever is true the divine intellect knows with certainty, because no truth can be hidden from an infinite intellect, and the divine intellect is infinite.

So, on their view, 'the certainty of God's foreknowledge is to be sought from two sources. First, from the infinite power and penetration of the divine intellect. Second, from the determinate truth of future contingents.' These are the words of the Jesuit Becanus in his Summa of Theology, volume 1, treatise 1, chapter 10, question 11, first conclusion.

source_text: XXXVII. Sed singulae istae sententiae non parva difficultate laborare videntur. Primo enim quod attinet praesentiam illam realem futurorum in aeternitate, quatenus, scilicet, censentur ab aeterno aeternitati ipsi coexistere, apparet eam merum esse commentum. Nam ut unum alteri coexistat, necesse est ut existat utrumque. Quod enim non existit, coexistere non potest. Ac proinde cum res contingentes ab aeterno non extiterint, ab aeterno non potuerunt aeternitati coexistere. Neque quicquam ad hoc juvat, ea quae praesumitur aeternitatis indivisibilitas. Nam ei quod nullam admittit in se divisionem atque successionem, ea quae in tempore fiunt coexistere successive possunt. Quemadmodum palum in aqua defixum & immotum non eaedem aquae semper circumfluunt, sed perpetuo novae atque novae. Neque magis necesse est quod aeternitati Dei aliquando existit, semper illi coexistere; quam necesse est ut quod immensitati ejus alicubi coexistit, ubique illi coexistat.
english: Each of these views, however, seems to face no small difficulty. First, take the real presence of future things in eternity, meaning that they are thought to coexist with eternity itself from eternity. This is plainly a pure invention.
For one thing to coexist with another, both must exist; what does not exist cannot coexist. Since contingent things did not exist from eternity, they could not coexist with eternity from eternity.

The supposed indivisibility of eternity is no help here. Things that happen in time can coexist one after another with something that admits no division or succession within itself. A post driven fast into a river does not always have the same water flowing round it, but ever new water. It is no more necessary that what exists alongside God's eternity at some time should always coexist with it than that what coexists with his immensity in some place should coexist with it everywhere.

source_text: XXXVIII. Deinde cum inter illa quae Deus futura praevidet, multa sint peccata, & moraliter mala, difficulter admodum intelligi potest quomodo Deus futura cujusvis generis praescire potuerit, in absoluto aliquo voluntatis suae decreto. Nam bona quidem Deus efficere & decernere potest, absque ullo bonitatis & sapientiae suae praejudicio: sed bonitati divinae repugnat, ut ad illa quae in se mala sunt, creaturarum voluntates moveat & praedeterminet. Quis enim dicere possit, Deum absolute & efficaciter, decreto quodam suo, Angelorum qui defecerunt voluntatem ad hoc determinavisse, ut se contra Deum superbia efferrent, & primorum parentum, ut neglecto Dei mandato, pomum vetitum appeterent, quin hoc ipso statuatur Deus peccati autor? Aut quis in animum inducere queat hominum voluntates aeterno Dei decreto, antecedente omnem quocunque modo praevisam voluntatis creatae determinationem, ad actus blasphemiae & odii in Deum singulariter determinatas esse, nec Deum tamen esse peccatorum istorum causam?
english: Next, among the things God foresees as future are many sins and moral evils. It is therefore very hard to understand how God could have foreknown future things of every kind in some absolute decree of his will.

God can bring about and decree good things without any damage to his goodness and wisdom. But it is contrary to the divine goodness that he should move and predetermine the wills of creatures toward things evil in themselves.

Suppose someone says that God, absolutely and efficaciously, by a decree of his own, determined the will of the angels who fell to rise up in pride against God. Suppose he says God determined the will of our first parents to disregard God's command and covet the forbidden fruit. Who could say this without thereby making God the author of sin? And who could persuade himself of the following? By an eternal decree of God, preceding any determination of the created will foreseen in any way at all, human wills have been determined one by one to acts of blasphemy and hatred against God. And yet God is not the cause of those sins!

source_text: XXXIX. Neque etiam intelligo quomodo futuri actus causae liberae, in ea certo praecognosci possint, prout consideratur in iis circumstantiis, quibus est ad agendum proxime disponenda; nisi praesupponamus, illi quandam sic agendi necessitatem imponi, ex objecti propositione sub talibus circumstantiis; quod secum quoque non parvam difficultatem trahit. Nam inde sequitur Adamo, prout ante peccatum affectus & dispositus erat, necessitatem peccandi impositam fuisse per tentationem quae illi oblata est, & circumstantias quae illam comitabantur: quod aegre admitti potest, quin videatur a culpa excusandus.
english: Nor do I see how the future act of a free cause can be foreknown with certainty within that cause, considered in the circumstances that are to dispose it most immediately to act. That could only be if we presuppose that some necessity of acting in that way is laid upon it by the object being set before it in such circumstances. That too brings no small difficulty with it.

It would follow that Adam, affected and disposed as he was before he sinned, had a necessity of sinning laid on him by the temptation put before him and the circumstances that went with it. This can scarcely be granted without his seeming to be excused from blame.

source_text: XL. Quod spectat autem quartam sententiam, quae divinae praescientiae certitudinem quaerit in infinitate intellectus divini, & in determinata veritate eorum quae contingenter futura sunt, nihil illa ponit quod certum non sit & indubitatum. Nam quandoquidem evidens est, divinas praedictiones de futuris contingentibus in scripturis extare, hoc ipso manifestum est, veras propositiones de iis formari posse: nec enim quicquam Deus affirmat nisi verum. Omni autem verae propositioni necesse est ut in re veritas respondeat. Et sic cum determinate & vere dici possit, haec & illa libere & contingenter futura, consequens est, ut eorum veritas determinata sit. Nec minus est evidens, posita veritate futurorum contingentium, illam ab intellectu divino, qui infinitus est, percipi & cognosci. Nam cum verum sit objectum intellectus, intellectus infinitus ad omne verum se extendit: alioquin hoc ipso infinitus non esset, sed limites & finem haberet, quippe qui non posset aliquam veritatem attingere.
english: The fourth view looks for the certainty of God's foreknowledge in the infinity of the divine intellect and in the determinate truth of things that will happen contingently. It asserts nothing that is not certain and beyond doubt.

It is clear that Scripture contains divine predictions about future contingents. That alone shows that true propositions can be framed about them, for God asserts nothing that is not true. Every true proposition must have truth corresponding to it in reality. So, since it can be said determinately and truly that this or that will happen freely and contingently, it follows that its truth is determinate.

It is no less clear that, once the truth of future contingents is granted, that truth is perceived and known by the divine intellect, which is infinite. Truth is the object of the intellect, so an infinite intellect reaches to all truth. Otherwise it would by that very fact not be infinite but would have bounds and an end, since it could not reach some truth.

source_text: XLI. Sed quamvis ista sententia nil nisi verum contineat, quaestioni tamen minime satisfacit, neque praecipuam difficultatem tollit. Quod enim hic maxime intellectu difficile est, illud est unde habeant contingentia quod futura sint, & ex mere possibilibus, ab aeterno in naturam futurorum transeant, ut sub ea ratione possint a Deo percipi. Nec enim ad aliud hic videtur recurri posse, quam ad divinae voluntatis decretum, cum ab aeterno nihil extra Deum extiterit, cui mutatio illa tribui possit.
english: Yet although that view contains nothing but truth, it does very little to answer the question and does not remove the main difficulty. The hardest thing to understand here is where contingent things get their being future from. How do they pass from eternity out of mere possibility into the status of future things, so that God can perceive them as future?
It seems that no appeal is possible here except to the decree of God's will, since from eternity nothing existed outside God to which that change could be ascribed.

source_text: XLII. Ac praeterea illud magna difficultate non caret, quomodo res quae supponitur pendere a causa quae est in se indeterminata, & quae illam tam non producere quam producere potest, certo tamen ab intellectu divino cognosci queat, cum sic nec in se, nec in sua causa certam habeat ullam existentiam. Nam intellectus divinus, quantumlibet infinitus, non potest videre quod non est, nec objecti sui naturam immutat. Neque vera esset ejus perceptio, atque apprehensio, si, ut aiunt nonnulli, plus cognosceret in causa, quam de facto in ipsa sit. Becanus tom. 1. tract. 1. cap. 10. quaest. 7.
english: There is a further serious difficulty. Suppose a thing depends on a cause that is undetermined in itself and is as able not to produce it as to produce it. How can the divine intellect still know it with certainty, when on this account it has no certain existence either in itself or in its cause?

The divine intellect, however infinite, cannot see what does not exist, and it does not alter the nature of its object. Nor would its perception and grasp be true if, as some say, it knew more in the cause than is actually there. See Becanus, volume 1, treatise 1, chapter 10, question 7.

source_text: XLIII. Itaque cum rem tantam scrutanti, undique se tenebrae offundant, & occurrant tricae ac pedicae, ex quibus nos non satis extricare valemus, nihil magis tutum & ingenuum puto, quam ignorantiam nostram hic aperte profiteri, & serio illud Davidis usurpare, Mirabilis facta est scientia tua prae me, & sublimior, quam ut assequi possim. Ac quanquam aliorum ingenia nolim ex mea tenuitate metiri, & super hac re modestam disquisitionem damnare; facile tamen adducor ut credam mysterium hoc ad ea pertinere, de quibus dicit sapiens, Altiora te ne quaesieris, & fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris. Nec mirum videri debet, si mens nostra tam angustis limitibus definita, percipere non possit qua ratione intellectus divinus, cui plane nulli sunt fines, ea cognoscat & attingat quae sunt a cognitione nostra remotissima.
english: Anyone who searches into so great a matter finds darkness closing in on every side, and meets tangles and snares from which we cannot properly free ourselves. I therefore think nothing is safer or more honest than to confess our ignorance openly here and to take David's words in earnest: 'Your knowledge is too wonderful for me, too high for me to reach.'

I would not measure other people's minds by my own feebleness, nor condemn a modest inquiry into this matter. Still, I am readily persuaded that this mystery belongs among the things of which the wise man says, 'Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too strong for you.'

It should not seem surprising if our mind, confined within such narrow bounds, cannot grasp how the divine intellect, which has no bounds at all, knows and reaches things that lie furthest from our knowledge.

source_text: XLIV. Neque etiam illud quicquam officit certitudini quam habere debemus, tum de Dei Praescientia, tum de humana libertate, quorum utrumque in scripturis certum & immotum fundamentum habet, astipulante rationis lumine, & quod attinet libertatem humanam, ipsa nostra experientia. Etenim quam multa sunt, non dico jam in rebus divinis, sed in ipsa natura, imo in nobis ipsis, de quorum existentia dubitare non possumus, & quorum tamen modum & rationem mens nostra inquirere & scrutari non potest, quin se in laqueos induat, unde ipsa se non potest expedire? Quid clarius quam esse lumen & visionem; sed quid difficilius quam penetrare atque explicare quae sit natura luminis, & quomodo fiat visio? Quid notius quam corporis membra solo nutu voluntatis innumeris modis moveri: Verum quam arduum est capere & docere, qua ratione istud fiat? Aut quid experientia quotidiana magis confirmatum est, quam mulieres praegnantes Phantasiae sola vi prodigiosa multa in foetibus suis creare; & quid tamen super ea re Philosophi commenti sunt, quod tantillum prudenti viro satisfaciat? Ac proinde si in rebus humanis, res ipsa certa esse non desinit, quanquam rei modus nobis incertus, aut plane ignotus sit; multo magis id locum habere debet in rebus divinis, quae sunt a sensibus remotae & mentis nostrae captum longe superant.
english: Yet this does nothing to weaken the certainty we ought to have both about God's foreknowledge and about human freedom. Each of them has a sure and unshaken foundation in Scripture, with the light of reason agreeing; and human freedom has our own experience besides.

How many things there are, not only in divine matters but in nature itself, indeed in ourselves, whose existence we cannot doubt! Yet our mind cannot investigate how and why they are without entangling itself in snares it cannot get free of.

What is clearer than that light and sight exist? Yet what is harder than to fathom and explain the nature of light and how sight happens? What is better known than that the limbs of the body move in countless ways at a mere nod of the will? Yet how hard it is to understand and teach how that comes about!

What is more firmly confirmed by daily experience than that pregnant women, by the power of the imagination alone, produce many extraordinary marks in their unborn children? Yet what have the philosophers worked out on the matter that would satisfy a sensible person even slightly?

So if in human matters the fact itself remains certain even when the manner of it is uncertain or entirely unknown to us, this must apply all the more to divine matters, which lie beyond the senses and far exceed the grasp of our mind.
